sourceLines.text: The snow leopard, one of the most elusive creatures in nature, inhabits a 3,500-
kilometre  arc  of  mountainous,  permanently  snow-covered  land  stretching  from
Siberia’s Lake Baikal to the Tibetan Himalayas. Found in the mountainous regions
of twelve Central and South Asian countries (including Russia, Kazakhstan, India
and Tibet), in summer they live above the treeline at altitudes of 2,700 to 6,000
metres. They are well-adapted to cold, so only in the harshest winter months do they
come down to the forests, to altitudes from 1,200 to 2,000 metres. Powerful, solitary
predators, they hunt only at dawn or dusk, and are able to attack and kill animals
three times their weight, their traditional prey being the bharal (or blue sheep) of
the  Tibetan and Himalayan mountains, which live  all-year-long at  an altitude of
around 5,000 metres.
Unusually for a big cat, their eyes are pale green or grey in colour, and they have
evolved  thick  grey  hair  that  insulates them  against  the  harsh  mountain  winters.
Their powerful legs allow them to jump as far as 15 metres, and their wide paws act
as a natural snow-shoe, allowing them to walk over snow up to 85 centimetres in
depth. They use their tails for balance, and as further protection against the cold. A
mature snow leopard has a weight of between 27 and 55 kilograms, with a length of
75 to 150 centimetres. Although snow leopards are a closer cousin to the tiger than
the  leopard,  they  differ  from  the  tiger  in  one  crucial  respect.  Their  legendary
quietness is the result of their larynx evolving differently to that of the tiger, and,
although able to chuff, mew, growl and wail, the snow leopard is unable to roar.
________________ (See question 8.) On the United Nation’s Red List of Threatened
Animals,  their  total  population  in  the  wild  is  estimated  at  from  4,080  to  6,590
adults, with a further 600 in captivity. Globally, they are subject to a number of
threats, which means they are faced with extinction. These threats are as follows:
climate change, the illegal trade in snow leopard furs and body parts, and finally
retaliatory killings.
As a result of climate change, our planet is becoming warmer. Average temperatures
are rising, and plants and trees that would otherwise not survive are now growing
at a higher altitude. Treelines are rising, and this is reducing the snow leopard’s
natural habitat and its hunting ground. The snow leopard is thus threatened with
starvation. The snow leopard is also being poached, primarily for its magnificent
fur,  which  commands  enormously  high  prices,  but  also  for  its  bones,  claws  and
meat, sold for use in traditional Asian medicine. Finally, there is the incidence of
retaliatory  killings.  Snow  leopards  are  coming  into  greater  contact  with  human
settlements. Increasingly, they prey on domestic animals and livestock, which has
led to their being killed by herders trying to protect their livelihood.

sourceLines.text: Travel writer Eric Smith goes to the North of England, visiting two of the seaside
holiday resorts he went to as a child to see if they are still worth visiting. The
conclusion he reaches is that they are not.
Monday: Blackpool
I’m standing on Blackpool Beach, and of course it’s raining. It’s a Monday in June,
and it’s too cold and wet to be on the beach, which, apart from me, is deserted. No
wonder then, I think as I trudge back towards the shelter of my hotel, that Blackpool’s
best days are over. The inhabitants of Manchester and Liverpool who  flocked here
during  my childhood have  settled  on  new  destinations  for their  summer holidays.
Helped by budget airlines, a guarantee of higher temperatures and no shortage of
good quality cheap hotels, they have moved on to Spain or Egypt. Who wants to visit
Blackpool when you can have Sharm El-Sheikh instead?
Blackpool  is  a  west  coast  seaside  town  which  has  seriously  declined.  The  shops,
those still in business, are clearly desperately short of customers, while the majority
have closed down. The town is not empty: when the tourists stopped coming, all the
formerly  thriving hotels  needed  new  customers,  which  they  got  in  the  form  of
unemployed people on state benefits, who would otherwise be homeless. They’re not
here for a holiday. They’re here because they have nowhere else to go. Thoroughly
depressed, I go to bed, to be greeted the following morning by a breakfast that, if it
were examined by doctors, would be banned as a primary cause of heart disease. I go
to the railway station and get on a train.
Tuesday: Bridlington
The train takes me 150 miles to Bridlington, an east coast resort town. As a child, I
would  be  dragged  here  on  family  holidays:  whenever  I  look  through  our  family
photograph  albums,  I  am  struck  by  the  image  of  my  family  sitting  on  the  beach
wearing  raincoats. On this June Tuesday, I am struck not so much by bad weather
(in contrast to Blackpool, there is at least some blue in the sky). What strikes me is
the number of old people.
________________ (See question 9.) The restaurants, the cafes, the shops, the hotels,
the streets, the beach, everywhere I look are people whose minimum age is 65. It’s
as if young people have been banned from the town, and can only be let back when
they reach retirement age. What happened was this: when tourists stopped coming to
Bridlington,  in  favour  of  holiday  destinations  in  Southern  Europe,  the  town
reinvented itself as a place for people to retire. That is why there are so many old
people’s  homes  and  specially  built  retirement  apartments.  Meanwhile,  the  young
people left  the town to look for better jobs  in Leeds, Manchester or London. So,
Bridlington as a holiday destination for families with young children? Forget it.
Wednesday: Back Home
I’ve  been  wondering  about  our  family  holiday  for  some  time.  The  last  two  days,
however, have decided me. I go to www.booking.com and reserve a holiday in Spain.

sourceLines.text: So why should you be excited about a new type of smartphone battery? This is why:
we have to stop burning oil, and we have to stop burning it soon. Twenty years ago,
the fear was that the planet’s fossil fuels would one day run out. Now, there is a far
greater threat: not running out of oil, but the consequences of using all the oil we
have. If we used all our existing reserves of oil, about 3 trillion tonnes of carbon
dioxide would be emitted, enough to raise global temperatures by more than 4 0C,
at which point it is not at all clear whether life on our planet would be sustainable.
Clearly, we have a problem.
________________ (See question 4.) Were that figure to be significantly reduced,
it would help in limiting rises in global temperature. How to do this? The human
race has to  wean itself off petrol-powered vehicles and start using electric ones.
Petrol engines must become a thing of the past.
Unfortunately, very few drivers want electric cars. This is because they are not very
good.  The  problem  is  not  the  electric  motors,  which  are  great:  efficient,  low-
maintenance  and  long-lasting.  It  is  the  power  supply,  the  battery.  Nissan’s
electric car, the Leaf, takes a lengthy 8 hours to charge. This charge gives a range
of  200  kilometres.  Including  both  driving  time  and  charging  time,  driving  from
KFUPM to Jeddah Corniche would take 66 hours. Renault’s electric car, the Twizy,
has a range of 100 kilometres (requiring a charge of 4 hours) and a top speed of 50
kilometres  per  hour.  In  this  desperately  sluggish vehicle,  the  journey  to  Jeddah
Corniche would take 81 hours. For most potential buyers of electric cars, speed is
not the biggest problem but, until manufacturers improve their electric vehicles’
range, nobody in their right mind would buy an electric car. This is where the new
device for charging your smartphone comes in.
In January 2015, a company called StoreDot unveiled a smartphone battery that can
be charged from 0% to 100% in 30 seconds. Company boss Doron Myersdorf says
that, within one year, they will have produced an electric car battery that can be
fully charged within 3 minutes; the single biggest constraint to the use of electric
cars will be gone. The charging time will be the same as that of a visit to the gas
station.  Electric  cars  will  become  practical  to  own  and  use,  and  we  can  start
consigning petrol engines to history.
How  does  this  battery  work?  Who  cares?  It  uses  something  called  bio-organic
peptide  molecules,  whatever  that  means.  The  important  thing  is  that  we  can
finally make the move to transport that does  not rely on oil. We can reduce the
amount of oil we burn, and hopefully sustain life on our planet.

sourceLines.text: Global warming and climate change are serious threats. Most scientists believe that,
if  the  human  race  fails  to  take  certain  steps,  by  the  end  of  this  century  global
temperatures will have risen by an average of  4°C. The World Bank has recently
published a study describing the potential  ramifications of this rise. What would
happen to our world if the global temperature rose by 4°C? The picture drawn is
terrifying. It feels as if it came from a science fiction or disaster movie, rather than
a scientific prediction that might come true within our own lifetimes.
Global average temperature is now .8°C higher than it was before industrialisation.
The world’s oceans have risen in temperature by .09°C since the 1950s, and sea
levels are currently rising by 3.2 cm per decade. Arctic ice caps and glaciers have
lost 400 cubic kilometres of ice in the last 40 years, and in September 2012, Arctic
sea ice reached a record minimum. These events are linked by scientists to a number
of extreme weather events, droughts and heatwaves (periods of time in which the
weather  is  much  hotter  than  usual)  that  have  taken  place  in  the  last  10  years.
However,  if  the  rise  in  temperature  were  to  continue  to  the  point  of  4°C,  the
consequences would be far more severe.
In a world in which temperatures have risen by 4°C, sea levels would rise by up to
1  metre.  This  would  bring  terrible  flooding  to  cities  and  coastal  areas  in
Mozambique, Madagascar, Mexico, Venezuela, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, the
Philippines and Vietnam. London and New York would face destruction. Some low-
lying  island  nations,  such  as  the  Maldives  or  Tuvalu,  would  entirely  disappear
beneath the sea, as would the United States city of Miami.
________________ (See question 6.) At the same time as regions near the sea were
devastated, the melting of glaciers in the mountains of India, Pakistan and Nepal
would reduce the supply of fresh water to these countries’ rivers, bringing drought,
crop shortages and famine as a result. Globally, food shortages and famine would
be a constant of a world in which temperatures have risen by 4°C. Millions would
either starve to death or die of illnesses caused by this malnutrition.
As the global temperature rose, summer heatwaves would kill millions. The 2003
European heatwave, which is believed to have cost between 22,000 and 35,000 lives
and destroyed $12 billion dollars of European agriculture, would become the norm,
repeated  every  summer  all  over  the  world.  Nor  would  heatwaves  be  the  only
example of extreme weather. The World Bank predicts a huge rise in the frequency
of events such as hurricanes and blizzards.
How  likely  is  this  prediction  to  come  true?  According  to  the  World  Bank,  it  is
possible to avoid a rise in temperature of 4°C, but only if decisive action is taken.
In  2010,  the  global  community committed  itself  to limiting temperature  rises  to
2°C,  but  whether  it  is  successful  in  doing  so  will  depend  on  the  actions  of
governments,  companies  and  individuals  around  the  world.  However,  as  of
November 2020, not enough action has been taken to avoid a 4°C rise. The question
we should possibly ask might be  when temperatures have risen by 4°C what will
the world be like?

sourceLines.text: The island of Martinique is located amongst the Lesser Antilles, a
volcanic island chain stretching from north-west of South America,
through the Caribbean Sea, to the West Indies. With a population
(as of January 2016) of 376,480 and a land area of 1,128 km 2, it has
existed  as  an  overseas  region  of  France  since  1815.  Part  of  the
European Union, almost its entire population speak both French and
Creole. Since 1638, the administrative capital has been the city of Fort-de-France,
located on the island’s east coast. Until May 1902, however, Martinique’s cultural
capital  was  the  town  of  Saint-Pierre.  It  was  in  this  month  that  Saint-Pierre  was
literally  obliterated by  the  eruption  of  Mount  Pelée,  the  20 th century’s  most
devastating volcanic disaster. On 8 May, 1902, Saint-Pierre was deleted from the
map. Its entire population of 30,000 perished.
________________ (See the appropriate question.) On 23 April, there
was a series of phreatic explosions, the heating of surface or ground
water by underground volcanic activity. On 2 May, residents of Saint-
Pierre witnessed a minor volcanic eruption from  Mount Pelée. The
following morning, residents woke to discover their streets littered
with dead birds, and the seas afloat with dead fish, all killed by toxic
volcanic  gases.  On  5  May,  a  mudflow  swept  down  Mount  Pelée’s
south-west  slope,  killing  150  people  and  generating  three  separate  tsunamis.
Horrifyingly,  a  plague  of  snakes,  rats,  insects  and  giant  centipedes,  escaping  the
conditions  on  the  volcano  slopes,  invaded  the  town  and  the  surrounding  areas.
Reportedly, about 50 people were killed by two-metre pit vipers, before they were
dealt with by local soldiers. Saint Pierre’s mayor, Roger Fouché, tried to calm his
town’s  panicked  inhabitants.  There  was,  he  reassured  them,  no  reason  for  alarm:
nothing bad was going to happen.
Between  07:30  and  08:00  on  8  May  1902,  Mount
Pelée  entered  what  is  described  as  a  declared
cataclysmic eruption phase. A pyroclastic plume (a
cloud  of  super-heated  gases  and  volcanic  matter)
rose  10  kilometres  into  the  air  above  Martinique.
The  skies  were  blackened  over  an  80-  kilometre
radius. Gravity then brought the plume to earth, to
Mount Pelée
the slopes of Mount Pelée, where it converted into
a  pyroclastic flow, descending down onto Saint-Pierre at a temperature of 400 to
600  0C. It is believed that 30,000 men, women and children lost their lives in an
instant.  Over  the  next  few  years, Mount  Pelee  remained  active,  its  final  eruption
taking place in October 1905.
According to legend, from a population of 30,000, there were two survivors. The
first was a Monsieur Léon Compère-Léandre, who lived on the town’s outskirts, and
Monsieur Louis-Auguste Cyparis, who had only survived due to his incarceration in
the town jail, following his imprisonment for wounding a friend with a cutlass. In
reality, however, there  were  other survivors,  most  of whom  owed their escape  to
being  far  enough  away  from  the  epicenter.  Many  were  badly  burned,  some
succumbing to their injuries in the following days.
In view of the terrible loss of life, we might nowadays ask why the town had not
been evacuated when there were so many clear warning signs of a coming volcanic
eruption. The answer is that at that point there had been little scientific study of
volcanic eruptions. The warning signs and risks were largely unknown. It was only
in the wake of the disaster that the modern discipline of volcanology was founded.
As for Mount Pelée, it has been dormant for the last 117 years.

sourceLines.text: Every year in September: at this time, students from all over the world are starting
their university classes. This year, however, is not a normal year. It is the September
of  2020,  the  year  of  the  Coronavirus  Lockdown.  Globally,  university  classes  are
online.  Both  Oxford  and  Harvard  Universities,  for  instance,  have  decided  that  all
lectures will be held online for the academic year 2020-21. This week, Uni Teachers
Monthly spoke to two university teachers (of course via Microsoft Teams, to maintain
social distancing) to find out how they felt about teaching their students online, from
their own homes.
‘It’s a far from ideal situation,’ says Eric Smith from the University of Drizzley’s
English  Language  Centre.  ‘Not  being  physically  present  in  the  classroom,  being
unable to see the whole class face-to-face, renders it far harder to gauge levels of
comprehension. You need to know if they’re getting it. Teachers do that by looking
in students’ eyes. You also require physical presence to judge and maintain student
engagement. It’s so much easier to keep students interested when they’re present in
the classroom. Being in an isolated learning environment makes it harder for students
to stay focussed. They’re much more likely to  drift off. Not only that, being in a
classroom isn’t just about learning. It’s a social experience for young people. The
friends you make there last your whole life. I feel sorry for the students in my class.
There’s  a  generation  of  students  losing  the  opportunity  to  form  social  bonds,
something that the rest of us took for granted.
________________ (See question 6.) Are there any practical issues connected with
that? ‘It is a nightmare,’ says Norman Jones, also of the University of Drizzley’s
English Language Centre. ‘I need a quiet place to work! Nobody bothers me when
I’m in my office or in the classroom. At home? The wife is always putting the washing
machine on, and it makes a  racket. Especially on the spin cycle. And my kids just
can’t  understand  that  this  is  not  my  private  time.  My  kids:  Daddy!  Daddy!!!
Daddy!!!!!!  There’s  a  spider  in  our  room!  Come  and  kill  it  NOW!!!  Me:  But  I’m
teaching! My kids:  We don’t care.  Come and kill it NOW!!!! I hate technology as
well.’ So is there anything good about teaching from home? Norman Jones considers
this, before offering, ‘Well, these days I don’t worry that I’ve got bad breath.’
So what lessons should we learn from the somewhat negative opinions offered by Eric
and  Norman?  Perhaps  we  shouldn’t  take  what  they have  to say  too  seriously. It’s
human  nature  to  see  the  problems  rather  than  the  advantages.  What  we  should
remember is this: in just a few weeks, universities were able to move lectures from
the classroom to online platforms. Education is continuing. Millions of students are
studying in a safe environment. This is astonishing. It is an amazing achievement of
which  universities  and  teachers  should  be  proud.  That  there  are  problems  with
teaching online is obvious, but it’s not much of an insight to say so. So let us not
allow the perfect to be the enemy of the good.

sourceLines.text: ________________ (See question 2.) Which are the nightmares that keep them from
sleeping at night, so they regret ever having come to university in the first place?
Stress over future employment, their finances and family worries would all feature
in a top-ten list, but the most stressful element of most students’ lives is probably
a single sheet of paper: the attendance register.
For many students, the attendance register is a matter of life and death. Come late
to class? You lose marks. Have too many absences? You lose more marks. Have
more absences? You get kicked out of the university.
But could all of this change? According to a report compiled by Professor Norman
Smith  of  the  Drizzley  Institute  of  Educational  Psychology,  attendance  in  class
should be cancelled, and the attendance register done away with.
Far  from  being  an  aid  to  education,  the  report  suggests,  it  could  even  be
counterproductive. ‘Attendance policy does more harm than good,’ says Professor
Smith. ‘Rather than helping students develop personal responsibility, it means many
students only come  to class  because they have  to. Were  we  to cancel  obligatory
attendance,  it  would  facilitate  more  students  identifying  regular  and  punctual
attendance  in  class  as  being  in  their  own  self-interest.  Not  only  that.  Taking
attendance wastes an enormous amount of time. Imagine how much more teachers
could do if they didn’t waste time on the register! Finally, there are many bright
students out there who simply don’t have good time management skills. Why are
intelligent students getting kicked out of university simply because they can’t get
themselves out of bed in the morning?’
However, the suggestion made in in Professor Smith’s report, far from meeting with
universal agreement, has so far proved controversial. Eric Green, director of the
National University Lecturers Association (NULA) reacted with outright hostility. It
is a scandalous disgrace!’ he said, when asked his opinion of the suggestion. ‘The
very notion of cancelling attendance is appalling. When I was a student, had I not
been forced to attend all those tedious classes, I wouldn’t be where I am today! I
would  have  been  kicked  out  of  university  long  before  graduation!  At  that  age,
students  are  too  immature  to  manage  their  time.  To  get  them  out  of  bed  in  the
morning, they need a great big stick, which is the register.’
So are registers going to become a thing of the past? Don’t get excited just yet.
Many students have reacted positively to the suggestion, seeing in it an end to their
stress over losing marks or getting kicked out of the university due to absence. But
it isn’t up to students. Their views are unlikely ever to be taken into account. So
given the angry reaction amongst many to the suggestion, the best advice to students
might be don’t even think about throwing away your alarm-clock.

sourceLines.text: On  19th  September,  1991,  two  German  tourists,  Helmut  and  Erika  Simon,  while
walking the  east  ridge  of  Mount  Fineilspitze  in the  Ötztal  Alps  at  an  altitude  of
3,210 metres, made an alarming and unexpected discovery. Protruding from the ice
were the head and upper torso of a man, the remainder frozen solid beneath the ice.
Believing the remains to be those of a recently deceased mountaineer, they alerted
the rescue services, and the following day, the first attempt was made to free the
body. Using ice axes and a pneumatic drill, local gendarmes tried to cut away the
ice from around the body, but had to abandon their attempt as the weather soured.
Alongside the tools and artefacts found at the site, the remains were only extracted
from the ice on the 22 nd of September, and then transported to the Austrian city of
Innsbruck, there to be analysed at the offices of the medical examiner. It was there
that  they  were  examined  by  archaeologist  Konrad  Spindler  of  the  University  of
Innsbruck. In an estimate that was to prove 1,300 years short, he announced that,
judging  by  the  style  of  the  axe  found  with  him,  the  remains  were  those  of  a
remarkably  well-preserved  4,000  years  old  Copper-Age  man.  DNA  testing  later
demonstrated that the body was in fact 5,300 years old.
It is now known that at the time of his death the Iceman (as he came to be known)
had  a  height  of  1.65  metres,  a  weight  of  50  kilograms  and  was  45  years  of  age.
Analysis  of pollen,  dust  grains and  the  isotopic  composition  of  his  tooth enamel
indicated that he lived as a child near the village of Feldthurns, north of the present-
day Italian city of Bolzano, but later went to live in the valleys lying 50 kilometres
to the north. Detailed analysis of his stomach contents revealed a diet of deer meat,
herb bread, roots and fruits. As for his occupation, the discovery of a high number
of copper  particles  in  the  Iceman’s  hair, and  his  possession  of  a  copper axe  and
knife, has led to speculation that he was a copper worker, involved in its smelting.
________________  (See  question  7.)  For  many  years  following  his  discovery,
there  was  much  speculation  over  what  killed  the  Iceman,  for
example, that he might have frozen to death or that he could have
got lost in the mountains. In 2001, however, X-rays and a CT scan an arrow
revealed that the Iceman had had an arrowhead lodged in his left shoulder when he
died, and a that there was a matching tear in his coat. It is now certain that he died
a violent death, dying of blood loss following his being struck by an arrow. DNA
traces from four other men have been found on the Iceman’s knife and axe, and there
is now speculation that he was killed at a lower altitude and then carried higher into
the mountains, possibly to conceal his killing.
Not only is the Iceman remarkable for being a well-preserved example of a Copper-
Age  man.  During  their  examination  of  the  Iceman,  scientists  made  another
remarkable discovery. Organised into 19 groups, on his skin there are 61 separate
tattoos.  Consisting  of  sets  of  vertical  or  horizontal  lines,  the  location  of  these
tattoos, on the skin over where the Iceman was suffering various ailments, has led
to speculation that these tattoos had a medicinal intention. Whatever their purpose,
the Iceman is also remarkable for being the world’s oldest known wearer of tattoos.

reached  the  eastern  United  States.  Hundreds  of  thousands  of  pioneers  began  the
journey  to  California.  Braving  the  dangers  that  lay  along  their  path,  blizzards,
rainstorms,  snowstorms,  tornadoes,  plague  and  attacks  by  Native  Americans,  they
risked all to reach the wilderness of California. The discovery also set into motion
one of the strangest stories of the American West.
________________ (See question 3.) In late 1848, when he heard the news of gold’s
discovery, Norman Donner was working at Boston Zoo as assistant zoo-keeper. Tired
of Boston’s cold, his low wages and long working hours, the Californian gold stories
inspired him to a new ambition. He, Norman Donner, would open California’s first
zoo. Those made rich by gold, he reasoned, would need somewhere to spend their
money. Where better than San Francisco Zoo? Along with other zoo-keepers, Donner
put his savings into supplies necessary for the long journey, wagons and food. He
also  bought  the  animals  that  were  to  form  the  zoo’s  stock:  seventeen  parrots,  an
antelope, a camel, a duck, a flamingo, a giraffe, an ostrich, a penguin, a swan, a
wallaby, a zebra, two yellow-branded poison rabbits and a kangaroo.
It was not until 1 st May, 1850, that Donner, his party of zoo-keepers and animals set
off on their journey. This was to prove a terrible mistake. According to those who
had explored the region, timing was crucial. Along the route they were following lay
the  Sierra  Nevada  Mountains,  whose  successful  crossing  depended  on  the  season.
Too early in the year, and mud and rain would block the paths over the mountain.
Too  late,  and  they  would  be  closed  by  snowstorms.  Donner  had  wanted  to  leave
earlier, but their departure had been delayed by waiting for an elephant, which had
been ordered but never materialised. If the elephant had been delivered on time, they
would have set off on time and their journey would have ended safely in California.
Instead, it was to descend into hunger, madness and finally horror.
They arrived in the Sierra Nevada Mountains in early November, 1850, to find the
mountain path blocked by heavy snow. Further progress was now impossible. As their
supplies dwindled, they faced starvation. Constantly hungry, the group looked around
them. Where could they possibly find food in that wilderness? Norman Donner had
to make a terrible decision.
The parrots were first, but they were scrawny, with little meat. Then the antelope,
the camel, the duck, the flamingo and the giraffe. 1850 turned into 1851. In January
they finished off the ostrich, the penguin, the swan, the wallaby and the zebra. In
February, two of their party became ill and died after eating the two yellow-branded
poison rabbits. Finally, in March 1851, they ate the kangaroo. They had run out of
zoo animals to eat.
When,  in  late  March,  they  were  finally  rescued,  their  rescuers  described  them  as
looking like ghosts. Norman Donner never opened California’s first zoo. Instead, he
accidentally found a large piece of gold and retired as a very rich man.

For years, the Native Americans had seen the wild

The atmosphere was extremely tense. On the advice of John Shangreau, a guide and
interpreter who spoke Sioux, the commanding officer, Major Whitside, decided not
to immediately take the Native Americans’ weapons. Instead, the Native Americans
were escorted 8 kilometres westward to a location known as Wounded Knee. There,
the  US  soldiers  and  Native  Americans  made  camp  for  the  night.  The  following
morning, the 29 th December, 1890, the soldiers surrounded the encampment of Native
American  men,  women  and  children,  and  demanded  that  they  hand  over  their

named  Black  Coyote  refused  to  give  up  his  rifle  because  it  had  been  expensive.

was  fired.  The  surrounding  Seventh  Cavalry  soldiers  opened  fire  on  the  Native
Americans.  What  is known  for  sure  is  that,  when  the  firing  stopped,  200  mainly
unarmed  men,  women and  children had  been  shot  dead.  25  US  soldiers  were  also
amongst the casualties, most of them almost certainly shot by their own side.
At  first,  this  incident  was  known  as  the  Battle  of  Wounded  Knee.  Newspapers
published admiring accounts of the ‘battle’ and twenty of the US soldiers who had
been there were awarded the US Medal of Honor. However, as the years went by and
the American public gained a more realistic idea of what really happened that day, it
came to be known instead as the Wounded Knee Massacre. It was the last example of
violent conflict between Native Americans and white settlers, the event that finally
broke the spirit of the Native Americans. The West had been won.

sourceLines.text: Ariane flight VA256: 25 December 2021, the Guiana Space Centre. At 09:20
local time, the Ariane 5 rocket took off from the launch pad, its twin engines
each delivering 7,080 kN of thrust, sufficient to propel its 777,000 kilograms
to  the  required  escape  velocity,  and  so  into  space.  After  27  minutes,  the
Ariane 5 reached an altitude of 250 kilometres, and released its payload: the
successor to the Hubble, the James Webb Space Telescope, the world’s most
powerful infrared telescope.

________________  (See  the  appropriate  question.)  An  infrared  telescope  is  one
which detects electromagnetic light: with wavelengths longer than those of visible
light,  it is invisible to the human eye and optical telescopes. Infrared telescopes’
particular use is in astronomy: all objects in the universe with a temperature above
absolute  zero  emit  electromagnetic  radiation.  By  using  infrared  telescopes,  they
become  observable  in  ways  impossible  for  optical  telescopes,  for  which  their
emissions of light are too weak or remote.
There are two types of infrared telescopes. Firstly, there are ground-based infrared
telescopes. These are infrared telescopes stationed on earth. Examples include the
Mauna Kea Observatory and the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope, both located in
Hawaii.  However,  there  are  two  problems  with  ground-based  infrared  telescopes.
This is that when infrared light travels through the earth’s atmosphere, it is distorted.
This distortion reduces the telescope’s sensitivity. The next problem is that, to work
properly, the telescope’s instruments need to be kept at incredibly low temperatures.
Warmth  around  the  infrared  telescope  distorts  images  of  external  electromagnetic
light. These problems led to the second type of infrared telescope, the space-based
infrared telescope.
For  many  years,  the  world’s  most  advanced  space-based  infrared
telescope  was  the  Hubble,  but  the  James  Webb  Space  Telescope
(JWST) is far more advanced. While the Hubble hosted an aperture
(an  opening  through  which  light  travels)  of  240  centimetres,  the
JWST is equipped with one of 650 centimetres. While the Hubble
has  effective  wavelength  coverage  of  0.2-1.7  μm,  once  fully-
operational, the JWST will have coverage of 0.6-28.5 µm. In every
respect, the JWST is a game-changer.
The James Webb
Space Telescope
An  unusual  development  with  the  JWST  (one  not  without  risk)  is  its  physical
location: while previous space telescopes were stationed in low-earth orbit, the JWST
is located at the Lagrange Point, a point in space 1,500,000 kilometres from earth.
Here, its 5-layer heat shield protects it from the heat of the sun, earth or moon, which
might otherwise reduce its instruments’ sensitivity, impacting its ability to observe
the remote universe. A potential problem is that, if there are any technical issues, the
JWST is too remote for a manned maintenance or repair mission, as have been carried
out  on  the  Hubble  five  times.  It  is  currently  in  orbit  with  a  periapsis  altitude  of
250,000 kilometres and an apoapsis altitude of 832,000 kilometres.
At the time of writing, 11 February 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope is not yet
fully operational. Its instruments need to cool to its operating temperature of near
absolute  zero  (-247  0C),  and  its  instruments  still  have  to  be  calibrated.  Once  at
capacity, however, scientists claim it will produce clear images of events billions of
light  years  distant,  and  therefore  billions  of  years  old.  Scientists  claim  that  the
images will capture the universe 200 million years after the Big Bang. It will become
not so much a telescope as a time machine.

sourceLines.text: On  January  24 th,  1848,  in  an  area  of  California  70  kilometres  north-east  of  the
present-day  city  of  Sacramento,  a  carpenter  by  the  name  of  James  W  Marshall
discovered  gold.  His  unexpected  discovery  was  astonishing.  In  the  waters  of  the
South Fork American River, Marshall had  come across traces of a seam of gold so
strong that nuggets could be picked up from the river bed. Marshall’s discovery, and
the Gold Rush that followed, was to change the history of the United States.
_______________ (See question 3.)  Officially, it had been part of Mexico, but by
an accident of history, it joined the United States on 2 nd February, 1848, ten days
later. California was then an untamed wilderness, home to 150,000 Native Americans,
6,500 Mexicans, and just 900 Americans. Today’s great city of San Francisco was a
tiny village, with a population of only 200. Marshall’s discovery of gold, however,
was to change California, and the United States, forever.
At first, the tales trickling back to the United States’ more heavily populated East
Coast, stories of gold nuggets the size of a man’s hand, of unimaginable riches just
waiting to be picked off the ground, were discounted as rumour, lies or fantasy. In
December  1848,  however,  the  president  of  the  United  States,  President  Polk,
announced in Washington DC that gold had indeed been discovered in California.
Gold Fever began in earnest. A rush of pioneers, eager for the riches they imagined
waited for them  there, headed from the East Coast to California. It was one of the
largest internal migrations in the history of the United States. In 1849, approximately
90,000  people  came  to  California  in  search  of  gold.  By  1855,  their  numbers  had
swelled to 300,000.
There were two main routes. Both were perilous and full of hardship. The first route,
the sea route, involved an 8-month 21,000-kilometre voyage, sailing over the Atlantic
the length of the American continent south to Cape Horn, round the cape, and then
sailing  north  over  the  Pacific  Ocean  to  San  Francisco.  Thousands  were  lost  to
shipwreck or disease. The second route, the land route, involved a 4-month 6,500-
kilometre  journey  west  across  the  United  States.  Thousands  more  were  lost  to
disease, starvation, attacks by hostile Native Americans or death from the extreme
weather conditions they encountered. Altogether, untold thousands died.
A few lucky pioneers did become rich, but the vast majority found little or no gold.
Their true legacy is the state of California they helped build. Although their dreams
of  finding  gold  went  unrealised,  they  became  shopkeepers,  farmers,  workers  or
businessmen. By 1856, the once tiny village of San Francisco had been transformed
into a thriving city of 57,000. The one-time wilderness had become a truly American
state.
